detailed_rationale:
Chalet Hotels owns a portfolio of premium hotels (Marriott-family brands) plus a fast-growing Bengaluru commercial (office rental/annuity) real estate arm. The quant data flags a large growth divergence -- 3-year revenue CAGR of 34.9% versus 1-year growth of 61.2% -- and this one is mostly a base-effect story rather than a durable acceleration: hospitality demand was still normalising off pandemic-depressed comparison periods in the earlier part of that window, and the company has also been actively adding room inventory (129 new keys added in Bengaluru in H1 FY26), both of which inflate the trailing growth prints without implying a 60%+ forward run-rate is realistic. Neither the 34.9% nor the 61.2% trailing figures should be extrapolated.

Looking at same-store operating KPIs rather than headline growth gives a more honest current picture: Q4 FY26 hospitality segment revenue grew only 3% YoY, and RevPAR actually fell 3% YoY to Rs 10,544 -- occupancy dropped 7.7 percentage points to 68%, only partly offset by an 8% increase in average room rate (ARR). That is a softening core hotel business on a like-for-like basis, even as the group's consolidated Q4 PAT grew 32% YoY to Rs 163 cr, helped by the smaller but faster-growing commercial real estate segment: revenue there grew 37% YoY to Rs 847 mn with EBITDA up 42% at an 83.6% margin -- a high-quality, high-margin diversification away from cyclical hotel occupancy.

With D/E of 0.64 and interest coverage of ~6.6x (typical for a capital-intensive hospitality/real-estate owner-operator), and a PE of ~30x, the valuation is pricing continued strong growth. Given the actual hospitality KPIs (RevPAR down, occupancy down) are softer than the headline growth numbers suggest, and only the smaller commercial segment is genuinely accelerating, the valuation looks to be leaning on the base-effect-inflated headline rather than the more moderate underlying trend.
recommendation_rationale: Already a quant-Hold; the growth-divergence flag resolves toward caution once same-store hospitality KPIs (RevPAR -3%, occupancy -7.7pp) are examined rather than the base-effect-inflated headline growth rate, which argues against treating this as a rescue candidate, while the genuinely strong and diversifying commercial real estate arm keeps this from being a harsher call.
summary: Chalet Hotels combines a premium hotel portfolio with a growing Bengaluru commercial real estate business. The very high year-on-year growth numbers in the data mostly reflect a low pandemic-era comparison base and new hotel capacity coming online, not a sustainable growth rate -- on a same-store basis, hotel occupancy and room revenue per available room actually declined this quarter, offset by higher room rates. The commercial real estate arm, though smaller, is genuinely growing fast at high margins. We rate this a Hold: a decent diversification story, but the headline growth figures overstate the underlying momentum.
positive_para: The Bengaluru commercial real estate (rental/annuity) segment is a genuine bright spot -- revenue +37% YoY, EBITDA +42% YoY, at an 83.6% margin -- providing a high-quality, less-cyclical earnings stream alongside the hotel business. Consolidated Q4 PAT still grew 32% YoY, and average room rates continue to rise (+8% YoY), showing some pricing power even as occupancy softens.
negative_para: The headline 1-year and 3-year revenue growth rates (61% and 35%) are substantially inflated by pandemic-era base effects and new room inventory coming online, not a sustainable trend -- and the same-store data tells a more cautious story: Q4 RevPAR fell 3% YoY and occupancy dropped 7.7 percentage points to 68%. A hotel business relying on rate increases to offset falling occupancy is a less durable growth driver than volume-led demand.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ~30x earnings, the valuation looks to be crediting the base-effect-inflated headline growth rates rather than the more moderate combination of a softening same-store hotel business and a genuinely fast-growing but still-small commercial arm. Fair-to-rich once the growth-divergence is properly discounted; not a name to underwrite on the trailing growth numbers.
